findings.claim: Names the exam board three times in student-facing prose: "Eduqas examiners expect you to know all of them", "Eduqas requires you to know four sampling techniques", "Eduqas does not just want you to name a method".
findings.truth: House rule: an Eduqas/WJEC lesson must never name the board in prose. The first phrase is also an invented examiner claim. The underlying facts are right: the spec examines all six enquiry stages and lists random, systematic, opportunistic and stratified sampling.
findings.evidence: spec pages 22-23 (enquiry skills 1.1-1.6; sampling in 1.2); house rule in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: "Examiners reward the word 'because' followed by a clear reason."
findings.truth: No published mark scheme rewards a single word. The advice itself is sound, so it is rewritten as guidance to the student rather than as a claim about examiners.
findings.evidence: no source; fabricated examiner claim (brief bans these)

findings.claim: Flashcard [1].q: "How many stages does the Eduqas enquiry process have?"
findings.truth: The board must not be named. "the geographical enquiry process" is the neutral form; the answer (six) stays correct.
findings.evidence: spec page 22, enquiry stages 1.1-1.6; house rule

findings.claim: Flashcard [9].a: "Measuring river discharge with a flow meter and timed float."
findings.truth: A flow meter or a timed float measures velocity. Discharge needs velocity multiplied by cross-sectional area (width x mean depth). The card is acceptable as an example of a quantitative technique, but a student could carry the shortcut into a method question.
findings.evidence: standard hydrology (Q = A x v); spec page 22 lists flow, e.g. discharge, as a quantitative technique

findings.claim: "Eduqas examiners reward two skills here.", "Eduqas requires you to know mean, median, mode, range, quartiles and inter-quartile range.", "The Eduqas spec stresses that 'geography can be messy'".
findings.truth: Board named in prose (house rule), and the first is also an invented examiner claim. Both underlying statements are correct: Appendix A 2.1 lists median, mean, range, quartiles, inter-quartile range, mode and modal class, and enquiry skill 1.5 does say geography can be 'messy'.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix A 2.1 (page 30); spec page 22 skill 1.5; house rule

findings.claim: On a line of best fit: "The slope shows the strength of the relationship."
findings.truth: The slope shows the direction and the rate of change. The strength of the relationship is shown by how tightly the points cluster about the line. Teaching 'steeper = stronger' is a known correlation misconception and would cost marks in an analysis answer.
findings.evidence: statistical definition of correlation vs gradient; spec Appendix A 2.3 (trend lines, lines of best fit) and 2.4 (limitations of a scatter graph)

findings.claim: "A <dfn ...>anomaly</dfn> is a value that does not fit the trend."
findings.truth: Wrong article before a vowel: it should read "An anomaly". The dfn tag and its data-def are untouched.
findings.evidence: English grammar; SPaG is assessed in this component

findings.claim: Mark scheme [5].marks: "Examiners reward use of specific figures from the data, which forces calculation, not just visual estimation."
findings.truth: Another invented examiner claim. The point stands as advice: quoting specific figures forces calculation rather than visual estimation.
findings.evidence: no source; fabricated examiner claim (brief bans these)

findings.claim: "If pedestrian flow drops with distance from the town centre, that fits the bid-rent model: peripheral shops attract fewer visitors than the central honeypot."
findings.truth: The bid-rent model describes land value falling with distance from the centre. Footfall is a cause of high central land values, not a prediction of the model, and 'honeypot' normally means a tourist site rather than a town centre. The link is a common classroom shorthand and is not itself mark-costing, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: bid-rent theory (Alonso); spec Table B uses 'honeypot site' for visitor attractions (page 25)

findings.claim: Names the board four times: "Eduqas marks both at the highest tariffs", "the Eduqas fieldwork paper", "The Eduqas spec stresses", "come up in every Eduqas evaluation question".
findings.truth: House rule bars the board name in prose. "marks both at the highest tariffs" is also unsupported - the spec sets no such ranking of question tariffs - and "every ... question" overstates.

findings.claim: "Tape measures stretch in heat." and the suggested improvement "Use a metre rule rather than tape measures to reduce stretch error."
findings.truth: Tape error comes from tension and sag, not from heat: a steel tape expands about 11 micrometres per metre per degree Celsius, which is negligible over a river channel, while a cloth or fibreglass tape stretches when pulled and sags when slack. Swapping to a metre rule makes long-distance measurement worse, not better; the real improvement is to hold the tape taut and level.
findings.evidence: thermal expansion of steel (~11.5 x 10^-6 per K); standard surveying practice for sag and tension error

findings.claim: "In evaluation questions, examiners look for the words 'reliability', 'accuracy', 'bias', 'representative' and 'sample size'."
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Rewritten as direct advice to use those terms, which the spec does support: enquiry skill 1.6 names accuracy, reliability and bias.

findings.claim: Flashcard [11].q: "Why does the Eduqas spec say geography can be 'messy'?"
findings.truth: Board named in a student-facing flashcard. The claim itself is right - enquiry skill 1.5 says learners should appreciate that geography can be 'messy'.
findings.evidence: spec page 22, enquiry skill 1.5; house rule

findings.claim: The unit never states the component's defining requirement, and never mentions Part B. Nothing in the three lessons tells the student that two fieldwork enquiries are undertaken in contrasting environments, that the board selects one methodological approach from Table A and one conceptual framework from Table B, and that centres are told which two at least two years in advance. Lesson 3 describes only the UK decision-making part.
findings.truth: This is an omission rather than a false statement, so no edit is written. Options: (a) add a short paragraph to lesson 1 setting out the two contrasting enquiries and the board-set approaches, and a sentence to lesson 3 on the conceptual-framework part - the fix that matches what the paper actually asks; (b) leave it, on the grounds that the class teacher supplies the enquiry context and the hidden lesson notice already points there. Recommendation: (a), written in neutral phrasing with no board name and no fixed approach named as always set.
findings.evidence: spec pages 21-23, Component 3 description and Tables A and B; assessment section page 27
findings.ruling: Requirement stated in the L1 exam tip.

findings.claim: "On a beach pebble study, 30 pebbles per site is a common minimum".
findings.truth: A teaching rule of thumb, not a spec requirement. It is hedged as 'a common minimum', so it is not misleading and is left alone. The spec only asks learners to justify sample size.
findings.evidence: spec page 22, enquiry skill 1.2 ('Justify sample size and sampling technique')

summary: Content, statistics and answer keys are sound: every knowledge-check key, match order and mark total is correct, and the sampling, graph-choice, central-tendency and inter-quartile-range teaching matches Appendix A. The unit's real faults are house-rule breaches - the board is named nine times in student-facing prose and flashcards, and four passages invent examiner claims - plus one correlation misconception (slope = strength), one wrong equipment claim (tapes stretch in heat) and a grammar slip. One ADJUDICATE: the unit never explains the two contrasting fieldwork enquiries with board-set approaches, or the conceptual-framework part of the paper.
